en: In the *Record of Mount Tiantai*, Xu Zhengjun compiled the account of Fangying Guan.
Sun Chuo stated: "If one traverses the sea, there are Fangzhang and Penglai; if one ascends by land, there is Siming."
Tiantai— how truly credible it is!
It is indeed a sacred pool within the vast expanse of heaven and earth.
Regarding the separate pavilion of the Three Clarities, according to the *Zhen'gao*,
Mount Tiantai is eighteen thousand *zhang* high and eight hundred *li* in circumference.
The mountain consists of eight tiers,
identical on all four sides,
and is situated within the divisions of the constellations Ox (Niu) and Dipper (Dou).
Because its summit corresponds to the Tai (Altar) lunar station and serves as a radiant assistant to the Purple Palace (the Emperor),
it is named Tiantai.
It is also called:
Regarding the ascension to the Perfected State by Tao Yinyu at Mount Qibai:
The *Yin jue* (Secret Instructions on Reclusion) states that the Greater and Lesser Tai Mountains lie at the center of the five counties.
These are Yuyao, Linhai, Chuxing, Juzhang, and Shan County; as for the Greater and Lesser Tais, they are six *li* from Mount Tongbai, extending as far as the Two Stone Bridges.
One first attains the Lesser [T’ai].
Traveling again for over a hundred li,
they found another large one situated at the highest point.
The herb-gatherer saw them vaguely;
the stone screens and rainbow-colored beams resembled paintings,
and he further beheld jade halls and golden palaces.
I gazed toward the bridge and saw lotus flowers there;
their form was as large as chariot wheels,
yet the flowers were so ethereal that they could not be clearly seen.
The terms "Large Terrace" and "Small Terrace" are named according to the relative size of the stone bridges;
this is based on such an explanation.
This refers to Mount Tiantai and Mount Tongbai,
which are adjacent to one another yet slightly different.
According to the *Changkang Qimeng Ji* (Record of Changkang’s Enlightenment):
Mount Tiantai is situated within the boundaries of five counties in Huizhi Prefecture.
It is not far from inhabited areas,
and the path passes by a waterfall.
Next, from Youxi to Zhe-shan:
Youxi is located in Tangxing County.
It originates twenty *li* to the east from Huading Peak and flows southeast from Fenghuang Mountain.
It joins the Great Creek of the entire county and flows into the Xi Jiang of Linhai Commandery.
Its waters are deep, and ahead of the ridge there is a stone bridge.
Gazing from afar, it does not exceed a foot in length;
yet, spanning dozens of paces across a precipitous abyss,
only one who forgets their own body can cross it.
Duzhe beheld Mount Tiantai,
lush and concentrated in its elegance;
two ridges rose majestically above the azure heavens.
There are jade towers and gem-studded halls,
as well as *yāolin* (celestial jade) and *lìquán* (sweet spring water)—
various kinds of wondrous objects belonging to the immortals.
If someone should happen to see it,
they might at that moment cut down the tree to mark its location;
however, shortly thereafter, it can no longer be found.
According to this record,
such a place of divine marvels is not something that can be beheld in a moment’s notice.
What the multitude of travelers sees now is likely not this bridge; furthermore,
at the higher reaches of the stream, no bridge is visible.
What the people see now is located twenty *li* west of the Xie Pavilion;
the stream flows through the borders of Shan County.
It is certain that this is not the bridge described by Changkang (Gu Kaizhi).
The prefecture has taken its name from the mountain.
It is said: "The prefecture is Taizhou;
its counties are subordinate to Tangxing, which is the ancient city of Shifeng."
In the second year of the Shangyuan era of Emperor Suzong,
it was renamed Tangxing County.
The mountain is one hundred and forty-eight li from the prefecture.
It is eighteen *li* from the county seat.
One end extends into the blue sea;
within it lies the Immortal Land of the Golden Sands.
Within Mount Tóngbǎi, there is an area approximately thirty li in circumference,
which is constantly covered by yellow clouds above.
The trees are emerald and azure;
the springs are stone marrow and golden nectar—
the so-called Golden Court Cave (Jinting Dong) mentioned in the *Zhen'gao*.
Mount Tian is Tongbai,
the seat where the Perfected Man resides.
This Perfected Man was Zhou Lingwang’s crown prince, Qiao.
His courtesy name was Ziji.
He delighted in playing the sheng flute,
producing the sound of a phoenix amidst the valleys of Mount Yi.
The Daoist practitioner Fu Jin received him and brought him up to Mount Song.
More than thirty years later,
he sought him but could not find him.
He once rode upon a white crane and departed from the world of men;
having been appointed as an immortal official,
he served as the Right Assistant to the True Man of Tóngbǎi and presided over the Five Peaks.
The Imperial Attendant came to govern this mountain;
thus, the *Zhen'gao* states:
"Jinling of Gucheng in Wu."
Beyond Mount Tongbai’s golden pass lies the numinous site where immortals attain perfection,
a blessed realm for nurturing the spirit.
The *Record of Famous Mountains and Blessed Lands* states:
"The great waves do not ascend here; the three calamities cannot reach it.
It further states:
Traveling south from the Dan River,
there is a confluence of caves;
one must pass through them.
The caverns of Mount Chicheng and Mount Danshan lead upward to the Heaven of Pure Tranquility (Yùqīngpíng);
they encircle three hundred li.
Dongmen is located within the borders of Le'an County;
it is the sixth of the sixteen celestial grottoes (*dongtian*) and is the seat governed by Maosiming.
The multitude of peaks rises steeply;
emerald barriers overlap one another,
scraping the heavens and soaring beyond the Milky Way.
As rising clouds give way to mist,
the mulberry trees burst forth with fragrant jade-like blossoms.
Flowers bloom amidst the branches.
Its radiance shines brilliantly;
the four seasons are like spring.
Phoenixes soar and divine luan-birds perch upon it.
Fenggu is where the "Tiger of Wen" lies hidden;
it stretches south to Jinyun and connects north to Siming.
To the east it borders the surging ocean;
to the west it connects with the Shan River.

It abounds in *chīng* trees, pines, and cypresses, where glistening pearls and accumulated emerald greens rest upon the layered cliffs; sacred radiance and numinous fungi emit their brilliance from within the secluded valleys.
As for the mountain mists concealing the sun’s radiance, it does not seek to vie with the Five Peaks for supremacy;
yet by examining anomalies and seeking wonders, one may well take the Three Mountains as its authentic model. Thus it comes to rest here.

From the Jin dynasty down to the Liang and Chen dynasties, all emperors performed the ritual of offering sacrifices to this mountain at the summer solstice; they buried treasures in its walls and presented precious gems as tribute, making this a regular practice.
The *Nei pian* (Inner Chapters) of the *Bofuzi* states:
None of these minor mountains are fit for the production of divine elixirs or the golden liquid (*suvarṇarasāyana*).
They all harbor the essences of wood and stone,
and aged demons (*rākṣasa*) of a thousand years can ruin one’s medicinal preparations.
Only Mount Song has slightly lost its status as a guardian, while Mount Jinyun and Mount Luofu are inferior;
compared to all other mountains, the Great and Small Tai Mountains are the true abodes of the divine spirits.
To assist others is a source of merit;
it is through this that one may cultivate the truth and prepare the alchemical elixir at the Terrace of Refinement.
Tiantai Monastery is located eighteen *li* north of Tangxing County,
at the base of the Waterfall Cliff on the southwest side of Dongbai Mountain.
An ancient topographical atlas states:
It was founded by Ge Xian Gong for Sun Quan, the ruler of Wu;
it occupies the most strategic and scenic location.
To the north is Song Wang Zhenjun.
To the northeast of the altar, the Vermilion Cloud Cave stretches on;
to the northwest, the Emerald Screen Rock is cast forth.
Thus, Sun Xingong’s "Rhapsody on Mount Tiantai" says:
The emerald screen standing like a leaning wall is this very cliff.
The Immortal’s Altar and the Emerald Screen Cliff rise high into the void, competing in their loftiness, while waterfalls cascade and gush forth from the western slope.
It was over a thousand zhang in length;
its appearance was like a white rainbow hanging from the heavens,
with flying silk cloth touching the ground.
Sun Xingong’s fu states:
"Cascading waterfalls fly down,
forming a boundary for the path"— this is precisely this location.
Surging waves and frothing foam rise near at hand, startling like overturning clouds;
the drumming of angry billows and the roar of thunder are heard from afar, delighting the spirit.
To the south, the waterfall flows for over a hundred paces before merging with the Lingxi Stream.
It flows through Xuán County and enters Línhǎi Commandery. Within the monastery,
one observes the central stream drawing in cascading water that meanders around the corridors and courtyards.
The ponds and marshes overflow with water;
fragrant iris and lotus flowers bloom, while creeping vines and bamboo intertwine in lush splendor.
Those who wander there forget to return.
This is the ultimate of magnificent vistas.
Looking one hundred and fifty paces to the east,
there was formerly the residence of the former Magistrate Liu.
It was named Zixiao Mountain Hermitage; looking south,
it gazed upon the azure ridges.
To the north it connects with Zixiao Peak;
on both sides of the peak are small mountains that rise steeply,
forming a continuous and undulating landscape.
To the northeast lies Danxia Cave.
Within the cave is the site where Ge Xian-gong first refined his elixir.
In the courtyard, he planted many auspicious gardens with lush *sheng* trees.
Its flowering plants, winding ponds, and surrounding marshes,
along with its medicinal gardens and cinnabar furnaces—
these too are wondrous sights of alchemical transformation.
The master’s name was Liu Bi.
In the thirteenth year of Emperor Xianzong’s reign, he was summoned from Shimen Mountain in Fuzhou by imperial decree and appointed as the Prefect of Taizhou.
Before reaching the mountain, he attended to his duties at the foot of the peak and prepared medicines; subsequently, his entire family concealed themselves as immortals in the Danxia Cave.
From there, he gazed out toward Tiantai.
One *li* to the west of Fabu Temple,
it was established by the śramaṇa Fashun during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
It is situated near the base of a waterfall;
the temple was named after this feature.
One *li* to the north, there is a rock formation.
It rises a hundred *zhang* high and is named Bai Zhang Rock.
Beneath the rock flows a sacred stream,
for which Sun Xingong composed a poetic rhapsody.

Passing through Lingxi Stream, one bathes to wash away the turbidity and constraints of the mind. At Xianlu Temple, the mountain stream is diverted through the kitchen, then flows back to encircle the corridors and courtyards.
To the south of the temple lies Jiufeng Mountain.
The mountain is over one hundred zhang high and six li in circumference;
it is also a branch of Mount Tiantai.
Its former name was Mount Jiulong;
in the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era, it was renamed Mount Jiufēng.
In the past, Wang Yishao [Wang Xizhi] and Zhidun [Lin] [resided here].
He frequently ascended this mountain to enjoy its magnificent views.
From Mount Tiantai, he gazed out.
The Northern Road leads to Tongbo Guan, a distance of twelve li;
the entire way consists of precipitous cliffs and zigzagging steps ascending upward,
with nothing but long pines and narrow paths.
Upon reaching the cave entrance of Tongbai,
the original prose-poem (*fu*) states:
"The *su* grasses grow luxuriantly, casting shade over the towering, long pines."
This is that very place.
From the cave entrance, after crossing a small ridge for about two *li*,
one reaches the viewing site, which overlooks a small pine-covered ridge.
Beyond the ridge, the terrain suddenly opens into several tens of *qing* of level plains;
rising on all four sides,
the peaks and ridges resemble city walls and moats.
This is where the divine immortals rest and where Xu You and Chao Fu held them in reverence;
were it not for those who inhale the depths and soar above the Milky Way, [who could reach here]?
How can those who perceive the premature brevity of turtles and cranes in their dreams find a place to dwell alongside Heaven and Earth in eternal duration?
This was formerly the site where Master Chu cultivated the Way.
Furthermore, Master Xu also established a meditation hall here.
The gatehouse was named Zhongfeng (Central Peak) of Yinzhen (Concealing Truth). In front of the hall, there were more than one *qīng* of fields.
To the east lies a stream called Qingxi (Clear Stream).
The stream flows into the fields and,
to the west, passes by three wells with soaring waterfalls.
Whenever visitors behold its wondrous scenery and extraordinary objects,
they are suddenly transported as if ascending to the Mysterious Capital (Xuandu) or arriving in the Imperial City.
Its construction dates to the second year of the Jinglong era of the Tang Emperor Ruizong.
It was established by Master Baiyun.
Master Bai was actually Sima Tian-shi;
his name was Zizheng.
His courtesy name was Chengzhen.
He was a native of Wen in Henei.
His life story is recorded in his stele inscription.
When the Master first arrived at Mount Huading,
he met Wang Yizhi, who had entered the mountains to pursue his studies.
The Master passed on his brush technique to Yizhi.
If you wish to study calligraphy,
you must be fond of listening to my words.
Now, receiving the methods of the brush is not like common practice;
one must first still the mind and then clarify it.
One should contemplate evening upon one's accomplishments, noting that the tendons and bones are close at hand while the vital energy and strength are required.
Furthermore, they must be maintained with equilibrium.
There is no difference between grasping the pen and reaching the point of application; once the brush is set down, it flows forth.
This is no different from throwing oneself off a peak;
do not boast of physical beauty,
but simply seek strength and firmness of limb.
If one is naturally handsome by birth,
one must not pass too frequently through the stone chamber on the eastern side.
This is the spirit of a strange beast.
It has received its karmic training in another realm;
should any ordinary person arrive there, they will surely suffer harm due to their karmic conditions.
It would shorten my life.
You should bring it here; he will not dare to refuse.
That stone chamber in the west is most serene and secluded.
The writing desk and inkstone are both complete;
the poems and books are all sufficient;
and pine blossoms and immortal fruits are available for your use.
In the morning, one may satisfy oneself with stone-pressed tea and fragrant springs;
in the evening, drinking and strolling idly, let the waters disperse one's emotions.
When weariness arises, one ascends the peaks.
Do not think of idle matters.
Since I have received your instructions,
how could I dare to disobey?
Having ascended the stone chamber once, he remained there for two years without fail.
By night he gazed at the moon by the pond;
by morning he cast his gaze toward the clouds and took up his pen.
Filtering one's thoughts,
one should strive toward this practice at dusk;
purify the mind and spirit.
One who aspires to master the methods of calligraphy must observe the turning of light and the shifting of shadows;
do not move the brush too frequently, but let it improve day by day and month by month.
It has been nearly a year since he began his studies;
in the first year of his formal training,
his calligraphy was like a snake awakening from its spring hibernation.
Fish leap in the cold spring;
beneath the brush, dragons fly and butterflies dance between the lines.
Though not yet peerless in subtlety, it is so.
He had already astonished his peers from an early age;
by the second year he began studying calligraphy,
resembling a crane traversing a spring forest.
Clouds fly amidst the jade;
the brush holds five colors;
the dots of ink are like tortoises.
His sinews and bones were interconnected like hanging golden chains;
by his third year, he was studying calligraphy.
Thinking this would be marvelous,
he subsequently wrote several sheets of paper and brought them forth.
The Master bowed twice.
He spread them out upon the desk;
at the mere sight of them, he turned pale with a look of awe and spoke in a loud voice to Ze-yi, saying:
Your calligraphy has not yet achieved any merit;
it lacks both structural integrity and spirit,
possessing none of the necessary strength.
If one were to follow this style of writing,
how could it ever constitute written text?
For now, simply practice calligraphy.
"If you have a moment, please come to the Immortal Hall;
there is no need for you to trouble yourself to visit me.
Yì responded with a greeting.
He immediately returned to the study hall.
After another three years of diligent effort, his work was completed.
The Master then praised Yi, saying:
I reflect that your calligraphy differs from that of other ages;
where it is light, it is not light,
and where it is heavy, it is not heavy.
Those who attain it are rare;
those who behold it are seldom encountered.
To advance a single word brings a reward of a thousand pieces of gold; to present a single character grants the fief of ten thousand households and the rank of Marquis.
Again he praised him, saying:
"Among all trees, the pine;
among all mountains, the peak."
The numinous crane is the most central among birds;
Mount Song is the most central among the Five Peaks.
I have ordered you to return to secular life.
You soar toward the crimson of the nine heavens;
you return to the world like a crane emerging from its cage.
After our parting, my heart has remained with you;
from time to time, I gaze afar toward the midst of the white clouds.
This was after you, Master, first entered Tiantai.
Emperor睿宗 issued an edict restoring the former title of Tongbai and requesting that the Master reside there.
The imperial decree stated:
During the Wu dynasty, Ge Xian-gong abandoned his hermitage at Tongbai;
the observatory is located on Mount Tiantai.
It is as if one hears that there was a person from Shifeng County.
They cut down pines and bamboos,
destroy and lay waste to altars and ritual sites,
and commit many acts of defilement and pollution.
Having died and revived several times,
he looked up to the officials of the prefecture and county, who were acquainted with Sima Lianshi,
and [sought him] within Mount Tiantai.
He demarcated a square area of forty *li* in a remote region,
designating it as a blessed site for the perpetual life of birds, beasts, plants, and trees.
He established a Daoist temple there and restored its former name.
When the Hall of the Celestial Honored One was first constructed,
five clouds appeared above it;
three of these were recorded by an excellent official.
This was done to record the auspicious signs.
In the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era, the Prefectural Governor, Lord Jià Chángyuán, and Mr.
Lǐ Xuánjìng, the Master of Mysteries, [arrived].
The one named Han Guang was a disciple of the Celestial Master.
He also erected a stele for the Imperial Preceptor Xuanzong;
the Grand Astrologer Que Shang composed the text, and the Hanlin Academician Han Zemo calligraphed it.
Emperor Xuanzong personally inscribed the title of its stele.
One *li* to the south of the temple, there is a stone altar consisting of a single tier constructed of a mixture of bricks and stones.
The square hall measures thirty-two *zhang*.
According to the *Dharmacakra-sūtra*,
this is when the Three True Persons of the Great Ultimate descended.
This is where Ge Xian-gong practiced the Way on Mount Tiantai;
it is here that he was moved by the descent of the Supreme Perfected Ones upon this altar.
It is also the site where the Perfected Master’s True Scriptures, along with their commentaries and annotations, were established.
The details of his deeds are fully contained within the *Abhiniṣkramaṇa-sūtra* (Benqijing);
they are not recorded here in full.
Below, to the southwest of the altar.
Upon the stone is an inscription in *lìshū* script,
recording that on this day,
Prefect Xu was instructed at the altar of the *qiǎo* ritual to bestow the scriptures of the Immortal Lord (*xiāngōng*).
The Real Man claimed his surname was Xu and his given name was Lai-le;
his courtesy name is unknown, as is his identity.
In front of the altar there is a pond.
It is named Jiangzhen Tang (Pond for Descending the True).
The pond is planted with many species of lotus and water lilies.
From one *li* south of the pond to the entrance of the cave.
More than one li to the southwest outside the gate,
one arrives at the altar of Lord Wang Zhenjun.
This Lord Zhenjun is none other than the Real Man of Tongbo.
There is a small hall where the ceremonial image of the True Lord stands solemnly.
It was established by Emperor Xuanzong at the beginning of the Kaiyuan era.
Seven Daoist priests were ordained to perform the rites of sweeping and maintenance.
In front of the Hall is a stone spring named Qixian (Sweet Spring).
Three paces to the south, a new pavilion for the Supreme Perfected One has been erected;
from its perch atop ten-thousand-fathom cliffs, one can sit and observe a thousand li.
Visitors ascend it and sit to gaze out over the level plains.
According to the records, the main altar is located twenty paces northwest of the Hall of the True Lord (Zhenjun Dian).
There is a stone altar, four zhang and eight chi square, consisting of a single tier.
It was paved with ancient bricks.
Today, when the prefectures and counties pray for relief from droughts or floods,
they all do so at this altar.
Twenty paces to the east of the hall,
there is another ancient octagonal altar.
From the northwest of the hall, one descends the mountain for three hundred paces.
He then arrived at the Three Wells;
one well is now blocked and filled in,
according to popular tradition.
Once, a bhikṣuṇī washed her hands and touched it; immediately,
it closed up of its own accord.
The two wells were so deep that their bottoms could not be perceived;
both were natural springs from heaven.
Once, there was a person of refined interests who...
He cast his fishing line into its midst;
the line was completely unwound, yet it did not reach the bottom. Some say:
Tonghai; alternatively called Haifu.
It cannot be described in detail.
During the spring and summer seasons, whenever rain is about to fall,
the currents surge and rush forth, gushing up like boiling water and roaring like thunder.
It was like the latent fury of a dragon or a ch'i hidden in the depths;
those who encountered it while traveling through that region were all struck with spiritual terror and trembled in awe at the sight.
In the district, there were instances of drought and flooding;
every year, the magistrate would record his sincere devotion and pray for fine weather or rain,
and there was no response that did not manifest accordingly.
It is also a place where the state has performed dragon-investment rites and sacrifices to pray for blessings.
Emperor Gaozong invested a dragon here in the second year of the Yongchun era;
Emperor Xuanzong did so in the twenty-fifth year of the Kaiyuan era.
By imperial decree, Wei Chen, the Director of the Bureau of Rites for the Grand Chancellor,
was ordered to carry a golden dragon and white jade tablet and cast them into the well.
This was in the first year of the Baoli era.
The Sovereign dispatched the Palace Envoy Wang Shiji, the Daoist Ritual Master Zhao Changying,
the Great Virtue of Taicong Palace Ruan Youxian, and the Hanlin Waizhao Lu Tongxuan.
On the thirteenth day of the fifth month, I arrived at the mountain.
While staying at the Tiantai Observatory,
I performed a sacrificial rite (jiao) and made a vow to visit Sanjing.
This is the Ryūheki (Dragon Wall).
Ascending about two *ri* from the west of Sankei,
there is a monastery named Bukkutsuin (Buddha Cave Temple).
The present Dao Yuan Guan (Monastery of the Source of the Way) is this very place;
it rests its front upon the Cuiping Rock and extends northward to connect with the Great Mount Tóngbǎi.
Cui Ping Rock and the Immortal’s Altar stand as twin peaks beside a narrow path;
their waterfalls descend from the heavens, half-hidden above the clouds.
Upon the rock is a pavilion from which one may gaze far across the level plains.
This place is also a site of extraordinary scenery.
Traveling seven *li* northwest from Tongbai Guan,
one arrives at the Jade Terrace (*Qiongtai*), which is situated high in mid-air.
From the Unsurpassed Jasper of Bai Zhang Rock,
the path to the Jasper Terrace is entirely deep with water and stone;
it is so precipitous that it cannot be ascended or traversed.
One must ascend the Immortal Altar;
only by taking the Tóngbǎi Road can one reach it,
whereupon one gazes levelly upon the Jade Terrace.
Looking down from below at the twin towers,
many travelers marveled that the Jade Terrace was not situated in the midst of heaven,
and that the twin towers did not emerge above the clouds.
It is just as if one were observing it from atop a mountain;
yet if one looks up from below,
the jade terrace appears to be no less than at the center of heaven.
The twin towers stand five *li* apart, flanking Yunxi Stream.
Verdant cliffs ten thousand *zhang* high rise in dense, forest-like array facing one another.
Exquisite flowers and graceful cypress trees sprout their fragrant buds, while rare birds and cloud-like beasts abound.
I composed "The Sound of Yang's Purity.
I once sought out the Yunxi Stream below the Jade Terrace, tracing it upstream;
traveling north for thirty li, I arrived there.
In some places the waters flow gently and shallowly,
level for three or five li; in others,
there are deep pools and cavernous grottoes stretching into the distance.
Its depth reaches a thousand or ten thousand fathoms;
the strange rocks are rugged and jagged,
and the color of the water is bright and clear.
Everything is clearly seen to its very bottom;
not even the smallest scale can remain hidden.
Those who enter this state do not even realize they have forgotten their way home.
It is not merely a cave-dwelling of immortals;
how could it be otherwise than this?
Five li to the northeast of Tongbai lies the residence at Mount Hualin.

This is a realm of refined clarity and spiritual stillness, where water and rock meet. At the beginning of the Changqing era, the Daoist Chen Zongyan, while practicing the cultivation of perfection, looked northward and saw a peak about five li away;
there lay the Fangzhi Mountain hermitage.
Above it is level ground;
sloping slightly forward, there is a pond several mu in width,
with a small island in its midst.
From the Khe-ji marsh, one gazes upon the azure peaks ahead;
behind them rises a cloud-canopy,
which is the name of the rear peak.
To the west it adjoins the Jade Terrace (Qiongtai), and to the east it is near the Flower Forest (Hualin).
This is the Spirit Mansion (Lingfu);
in the first year of the Changqing era, he established his quarters here.
This is the second stage of Tiantai.
Seven *li* up from Fangxi Peak lies the abode of Mount Yuxiao.
The ground is level while the remaining four mountains surround it;
moreover, its seclusion is like that of a celestial grotto.
This is the third terrace of Mount Tiantai.
Traveling three li southeast from Yuxiao,
there are two stone ravines arranged like a lofty gate,
approximately one hundred *ren* in height.
For this reason, it was called Shimen (Stone Gate).
To the north of Tongbai Guan, there is also a path leading up to Huading Peak;
the road is deep, narrow, and treacherous.
Travelers rarely encounter one another;
for this journey, it is mostly taken along the road to Guoqing Temple.
From the Tian Tai Observatory, travel fifteen li westward.
There is Baiyan Temple.
The temple is thirty li from the county seat.
It was a shrine seen by the monk Puliáo during the end of the Song dynasty.
Traveling fifteen li eastward from Mount Tiantai,
there is Mount Chicheng.
The mountain rises three hundred zhang in height.
It is seven *li* in circumference and is the Southern Gate of Tiantai Mountain.
From ancient times to the present, it has served as the site for the state’s incense offerings and sacrifices.
The mountain is composed of piled rocks whose color is a brilliant crimson, like the morning glow.
Viewed from afar, it resembles the battlements of a city wall;
therefore, it is named Chicheng (Crimson City).
It is also called "Burning Mountain.
Thus, the prose-poem (fu) says:
"Red Crag rises like a sunset cloud, establishing its landmark."
This is that very mountain. On the mountainside is Feixia Temple (Flying Aurora Temple),
which was the residence of the Queen Mother of the Liang Peak.
Now it has been abandoned.
At the foot of the mountain there is a stone chamber where a Daoist practitioner resides.
At the foot of the central mountain is a temple called Zhongyan Temple;
it was established by the eminent monk from the Western Regions, Bai Daoyou.
Guoqing Temple is located ten li north of the county seat.
Tall pines line both sides of the path leading to the temple.
The temple was established in the eighteenth year of the Kaihuang era during the reign of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty.
It was founded by the Chan Master Zhiyi.
The monastery has five peaks;
the first is Eight Camellia (Bāguì) Peak.
Second is Yingxia Peak;
third is Lingzhi Peak;
fourth is Lingqin Peak.
Fifth is Xiangyun Peak;
the two mountain streams embrace it from both sides. Among the four most extraordinary temples under heaven, Guoqing is the foremost wonder.
Above the temple is the Tuṣita Terrace;
to the east of the terrace is a stone altar,
in the center of which is a spring.
In the past, Chan Master Puming struck it open with his mendicant’s staff;
thus it was named Xizhangquan (Mendicant’s Staff Spring).
[The spring flows] from Guoqing Temple.
Fifteen li to the northeast,
there is Chanlin Temple.
This temple is where Master Zhiyi originally practiced meditation.
In the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era,
by means of an official dispatch, the name of the abandoned Chanlin Temple in Huangyan County was transferred and exchanged for the title of Daochang.
Fifteen li to the east of the temple is Mount Xianglu (Incense Burner Peak).
It is exceedingly high and precipitous;
atop the peak, many fragrant cypresses, tamarisks, and cassias grow in continuous succession.
There is Yanzuo Peak (Seated Meditation Peak).
This peak is over one hundred zhang high;
it is the peak where the Great Master Zhiyi subdued the māras.
Later, a divine being sent the Stone Screen Peak (Shípíngfēng) to stand behind the Great Master;
it remains there to this day.
Beneath the peak lies a dragon pool.
It is one *li* in circumference.
Its waters flow down into Luoxi, which also empties into the main river of the county.

Ten *li* up the northwest from the temple, one reaches Chen-tian (Chen’s Field). Formerly, a divine person opened this field to provide for Master Zhizhe; he would sow in the morning and reap by evening. Five *li* west from Chen-tian, one enters [the valley].
One source was extremely level and was called白沙 (Baisha).
A monk resided there.
Twenty-five *li* up the northwest from Chanlin Temple, one reaches Xieting;
this is where Meng Gongjian of Pingchang served as Provincial Inspector (*lian-cha*) for the northeast region of Zhejiang for ten *li*.
It extends even to Lingxu, where those who come are received;
this is the Zen monastery of the wise,
the very place where Master Baiyun resided.
In his early years, the Master followed the Way and first resided at Mount Song and Mount Hua;
yet he remained entangled in the dust and turmoil of the world, unable to fully indulge in the appreciation of its seclusion.
He then traveled east to Mount Tai;
as it perfectly accorded with his long-held aspirations, he established there a place for the cultivation of the Real.
The Imperial Edict states:
Within Mount Tiantai lies the immortal precinct of the Lord,
a sacred site for the perfection of dhyāna,
which is constantly shrouded by yellow clouds.
This is its site; therefore,
he constructed the Hall of Contemplating Truth,
which was also named the Yellow Cloud Hall.
In the hall there is a small stream;
to the south is a ridge whose contours curve and converge.
In front of the ridge is a level plain.
A single-tiered altar is erected there,
constructed by paving it with stone.
It is named the White Mysterious Spirit (Báixuánshén).
Thus, the "Eulogy on the Sacred Site" (Língxū Sòng) composed by the Former Master states:
"The hall is titled Yellow Clouds (Huángyún) for its true qi."
The altar is named Xuanshen;
gazing upward at its pure radiance,
the eastern side serves as the chamber for refining punishments.
It attracts those who dwell therein.
To the south is the Terrace of the Phoenix’s Pivot,
used for chanting the wind and performing music with full vigor.
To the west is the Hall for the Quiescent Opening of the Invocation of the Deities;
to the north is the Pavilion of the Dragon Scroll,
wherein one may gaze upon the clouds and study the model calligraphy.
Though humble, it is not shabby and can withstand wind and rain;
though modest, it is not meager and can preserve the sacred vessels.
Ten paces before the white altar—
There is a large stream that originates from the southeast of Huading Peak and flows through the borders of Ninghai.
Furthermore, ten paces to the west of the hall there is a spring;
its color is clear and its taste sweet, capable of curing illnesses.
In the center of this level ground stands a separate courtyard.
He constructed a large alchemy furnace and cultivated a sword and mirror;
both were successfully completed.
There are ten tall pine trees and several clusters of long bamboo,
all of which were planted by the Master’s own hand.
Imperial edicts were issued repeatedly,
yet the Master declined them all.
This continued until the second year of the Jingyun era of Emperor睿宗 (Rui-zong).
Now my elder brother, Chengwei, has gone to the mountain to welcome you.
The imperial edict states:
"The Virtue of the Master exceeds that of the River Goddess."
His Way transcends the mundane and the near;
he wanders loftily at the heights of the azure void.
He walks alone upon the pure source, the realm of ultimate reality.
When I first ascended the precious throne,
I long relied upon your humble wisdom;
though I am not a Yao or a Shun, [I am grateful for your guidance].
With a mind yearning for the Great Plan, I call to mind Xi Que and Xuan Yuan; as they reigned over their eras, I look back with longing upon Mount Kongtong.
Reflecting on those who cherished tranquility, how could this hinder my gaze?
Morning and evening I stand in reverence and wait.
Although his physical traces remained behind, his mind was already soaring away; he wished to dispatch a messenger to welcome him,
but fearing that the Master might be startled or alarmed,
he ordered Chengwei to go and issue the summons.
I wish that you would come together with me to don the saffron robes before long; do not harbor such anxieties beforehand.
Before long, the Master was summoned to the capital.
The Emperor questioned him regarding the principles of governing oneself through purity and loftiness.
"If one values governing the state, what should be done?
The former master replied,
"The state is like the body."
"The body is like a state.
The Old Lord said:
"Let the mind roam in discourse."
He harmonized his vital energy with the Han,
following the natural course of things without any private will.
And thus the world is well-governed.
The *I Ching* says:
"The great man is in harmony with Heaven and Earth."
Such is the knowledge of its virtue:
Heaven speaks not, yet it is trusted;
it acts not, yet things are accomplished.
"The principle of non-action is the way of the family.
The Emperor sighed and said,
"How can the words of Guangcheng surpass this?"
He requested permission to return to the mountains.
The Emperor bestowed upon him a precious lute and a *xiawen* (cloud-patterned) robe.
Among the scholars of the court who composed verses on the *peì*, there were over a hundred;
the Emperor subsequently established Tongbai Guan for the various masters to reside in.
Traveling twenty li south from Lingxu,
there is a small village situated by the Huan River.
This was where the Liang dynasty scholar Gao Shi Gu Huan once resided.
This is called Huankui (Joyful Stream).
Traveling fifteen li west from Xieting, one reaches Shiqiao (Stone Bridge) along the Xianjian (Stringed Ravine).
At its head is a small pavilion;
the stone bridge is entirely clear in color and measures seventy feet in length.
The southern end is seven feet wide;
the northern end is two feet wide.
It has the form of a dragon and the back of a tortoise.
It spans a precipice ten thousand *ren* high;
above it are two mountain streams that merge and flow beneath the bridge.
It flows down as a waterfall.
To the west, it exits into the borders of Shan County.
Looking up from below:
Like a rainbow drinking from a mountain stream,
the bridge’s form is steep and precipitous,
and the sound of the water is a crashing roar.
Those who passed by at that time experienced dizziness and palpitations;
what travelers see today is precisely this Northern Bridge,
the place where the Arhat resided.
If one considers [the realm] to be merely small,
then one does not know where the great lies;
for the divine immortals are hidden in the profound mystery.
It is not something seen by ordinary people.
Following this bridge along the stream for fifteen li,
there is another stone bridge.
Zhongduan is known as Duqiao (The Severed Bridge).
Traveling twenty li north from Xieting, one reaches Huading Peak;
this is the highest point of Mount Tiantai to the north.
It is constantly obscured by clouds, mist, and haze;
there are few occasions of clear weather.
Its height is modest and its range slight.
Resembling the lingering clouds of late autumn, it gathers in the secluded ravine and remains frozen through the summer without melting;
when fair weather arrives,
one observes the direction of the sun at dawn.
The Shetu jing states:
"Master Baiyun traveled between the two locations of Lingxu and Huading;
from that time onward, his visits and prostrations were never-ending."
Above this, he constructed a Hall for the Celestial Honored One,
with two side chambers on either side, each opening a cavity to receive the sun and moon;
they partook of its light at morning meals and used the niches to store clouds and mists.
At evening, one inhales its air; before the hall stands a three-tiered altar.
Inside the hall is a stone statue, and atop a stone chime are an iron incense burner and a bell.
The northern altar has long been overgrown with brambles, though it was recently cleared and restored.
Ten paces to the east of the hall,
there is a sweet spring.
The Master resided there for twenty-eight years.
Although he was repeatedly summoned by imperial edict, he mostly did not comply.
The memorial states:
"If even laypeople who maintain integrity and remain in seclusion are permitted to dwell in lofty retirement,
it is only fitting that Daoists who cultivate the truth should yield to those far more eminent."
Furthermore, an imperial edict stated:
"Though we are separated by his [the envoy's] intentions, you should follow this directive; please transmit the petition that arrives here without duplicity or inconsistency.
In the eleventh year of the Kaiyuan era, Emperor Xuanzong summoned him into the palace.
The Master declined and returned home.
The Emperor, considering that Tiantai was remote and difficult to invite him there,
subsequently selected a site of superior geomantic advantage at Shangwu Mountain.
A special balcony was erected for him to dwell and observe;
joining this with Lingxu and Huading,
there were no longer any other halls or buildings.
Only pines and bamboos remained.
On a clear day, gazing out,
one could see the sea water, a brilliant azure color.
I am thus of one radiance with Heaven.
As for those of pure and genuine virtue,
the Three Mountains and Ten Continents appear to them as if before their eyes.
Cloud-belted pendants and wind-whistling flutes were suddenly heard.
From the summit of Huading, the path descends directly downward with extreme peril,
through thousands of cliffs and myriad peaks, where a thousand rain-storms fall upon a maze of overlapping ravines.
Monkeys and langurs leap and soar there, and spirits and deities take refuge; it is not a place reachable by human tracks.
Furthermore, located to the north of Mount Tiantai, it is at the Jinling Guan in Shan County.
Looking ahead, there is Xianglu Peak;
beneath the peak is a small cave that can be peered into.
Thus, there is no limit to its depth.
To the northwest of Mount Tiantai, there is a peak that rises solitary and steeply, facing directly across from Tiantai.
It is called Tianmu Peak.
The peak overlooks the road to Shan County;
looking up at it, it appears as if suspended above the heavens.
It formerly belonged to Linhai Commandery,
but was subsequently subordinated to Kuaiji.
Furthermore, there are two peaks known as Dacuī (Great Spitting) and Xiaocuī (Small Spitting).
Going toward Tianmu, one spits and it becomes a valley.
On Mount Tianmu there is a stone bridge that connects with Tiantai.
Upon the stone wall there are inscriptions in the *kōdō* script;
these too are so lofty and remote that they cannot be discerned.
Those performing the moon-sacrifice hear the sounds of the *jia*, the flute, and the drum.
During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty,
the Imperial Court dispatched all available craftsmen to carve the mountain's likeness onto round fans in order to manifest its spiritual wonders.
This is the place where Liu and Ruan, two men from the time of Xia Yu, encountered immortals while gathering medicinal herbs.
According to ancient accounts, the people of Shan named Liu Cheng and Ruan Zhao entered the mountains and met immortals here.
These matters are also fully recorded in his original biography.
Furthermore, according to the *Celibate Immortal Scriptures* (*Xianjing*), it says:
On this mountain there is a stone bridge;
it appears in one place, yet its location is unknown in another.
Furthermore, it is said:
The Rishi Bahudhāna encountered the bridge and immediately met [the Buddha] there;
for this reason, it is known as the Bridge of the Divine Seer (Rishi).
This is not something seen by ordinary people of the present day;
unless one’s sincerity is profound and reaches the mysterious, and the barriers that separate them from their counterparts are severed,
even true immortals cannot be seen.
The bridges, too, are well worth beholding.
As for the birds and strange beasts that dwell there, they exist in thousands of forms and myriad species beyond description.
Divine flowers and immortal herbs grow secretly within the valleys.
None can name them; yet the five fungi radiate their colors, appearing only when one is not of the True,
while the Jian tree conceals its shadow.
How could this be merely an ordinary observation?
In the tenth year of the Yuanhe era, the Lingfu moved his residence from Mount Chong to Mount Tai; when he first settled in his meditation chamber, it was still damp and drafty.
By the beginning of the Baoli era, more than two intercalary months had passed. During my leisure time from practicing the Way of Perfection,
I have briefly gathered from the scriptures and edicts to compose this record,
in order to manifest its spiritual efficacy.
*Record of Mount Tiantai*, one fascicle. *Explanatory Notes on the Zhizhai Book Catalogue*. *Record of Mount Tiantai*, one fascicle, compiled by the Tang dynasty Daoist Xu Lingfu.
He was a man of the Yuanhe era.
While I was serving as the acting governor of Linhai, I sent an official to the local province.
In the tenth month of the Bingshen year of the Jiaxi era, I resigned my command of the prefecture and proceeded toward the administrative seat of Kuaiji; on the way, I passed by his dwelling.
He was eager to travel there for a tour,
but as heavy snow fell, his plans were thwarted;
he instead turned his carriage onto the postal road and arrived.
I now regard this as a regret.
Having happened upon this record, I have transcribed it to convey my sentiment of "reposing in travel" (wo-you).
